Rayobyte is the better value for volume scraping: $35 for 10 GB against $40, about $200 for 100 GB against $360, and traffic that never expires. Infatica is the better choice when you need SOCKS5 (Rayobyte's residential gateway lacks it), ZIP-level targeting, IPv6 residential IPs, or ISO-backed sourcing documentation for procurement, and its $4 seven-day trial makes it easy to test first. Price-led teams pick Rayobyte; precision- or compliance-led teams pick Infatica.

Rayobyte and Infatica are both established mid-market providers selling residential, datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies. Rayobyte competes on price and flexibility, with non-expiring residential traffic that falls to $0.90/GB at a terabyte. Infatica competes on precision and assurance, with ZIP targeting on every plan, SOCKS5, an IPv6 residential pool and a strong ethical-sourcing story. This comparison weighs those strengths for scraping, local data collection and compliance-sensitive buyers.

blocks.text: Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte is a US proxy company that started life as Blazing SEO and built its name on dedicated datacenter proxies. Residential proxies have since become its main product. It sells them pay-as-you-go in four volume bands with traffic that never expires, sources at least part of its residential pool in-house, and offers country, region and city targeting. The notable limit is protocol support: its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5 or UDP.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica pitches itself on ethical sourcing and features available to every customer. All residential plans include country, city and ZIP targeting, IP whitelisting and selectable rotation times, and a 7-day $4 trial lowers the risk of testing. Independent reviewers have found its proxies fast and its pool modest but respectable. Its niche extra is a premium IPv6 residential pool, rare in this market, at about 1.5x the normal per-GB price.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Pricing: Rayobyte vs Infatica
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $35 with Rayobyte and $40 with Infatica: a 12% saving in Rayobyte's favour. At 100 GB a month, Rayobyte is the cheaper option at about $200 against $360 for Infatica, roughly 44% less. The sticker price is only half of it. Rayobyte's unused traffic carries forward, while Infatica's does not (subscription traffic resets monthly), so if your usage swings from month to month Rayobyte can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published' and Infatica lists '35M-40M'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Rayobyte lists Global countries and Infatica lists 195. On targeting, Rayobyte offers country, region and city, while Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. Infatica supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in Infatica's favour. On sessions, Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available, and Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Rayobyte: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires. With Infatica: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests. Run the same small test on both before committing.
SERP and rank tracking: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: ZIP targeting helps local search results. How Rayobyte compares: usable, with no dedicated SERP product.

Social media and multi-account management: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Rayobyte: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools. With Infatica: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature. Run the same small test on both before committing.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. Infatica: ZIP-level targeting for local prices. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing. How Rayobyte compares: fewer carrier or ASN controls.
Tight budgets: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. The limitation on the Infatica side: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Verification and payment rules differ too. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Rayobyte and Infatica before you commit
The quickest way to choose between Rayobyte and Infatica is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Rayobyte: check current offer; Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile)).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Rayobyte comes out ahead in 1, Infatica in 2, and 3 are ties. That makes Infatica the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget, while Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
